title: Custodian RBAC orchestrator and sidecarless authorization adapter
creator: Aisha Khan
description:
Summary:
Implement a production-grade RBAC v2 orchestration layer ("Custodian") that compiles declarative role/permission graphs into a compact decision model and provides a sidecarless authorization adapter for API/runtime/console traffic. The adaptor must support expressive conditional rules, low-latency decision paths, audit hooks for every decision, SSO/SAML session context propagation, and admin controls for emergency overrides and canary rollouts.

Goals:
- Provide a single codepath for policy compilation that can emit two artifacts: a fast in-memory decision graph for runtime enforcement and a compact audit-friendly trace for storage.
- Avoid mandatory sidecars: integrate the enforcement shim into our API gateway and runtime middleware to reduce deployment complexity for Dedicated/Hosted customers while supporting optional sidecar helpers for Private deployments.
- Ensure observable, explainable denies with per-request evidence for console UIs and operator debugging.
- Support session attributes from SSO/SAML (assertion mapping to subject, groups, org) and make attribute-mapping configurable per-tenant.
- Deliver fallback and safe-mode admin controls (global allowlist, emergency breakglass with audit and TTL).

Design highlights and trade-offs:
- Decision graph compiler: We will translate declarative RBAC v2 rules to a directed acyclic graph optimized for common fast-paths (token-based service-to-service calls, API tokens, session-based console). This reduces repeated traversal overhead. Trade-off: increased complexity in compilation pipeline vs. large runtime perf win.
- Sidecarless enforcement: embedding enforcement into gateway/runtime reduces network hops and simplifies ops for Hosted; downside is tighter coupling to gateway releases. Mitigation: keep enforcement implementation small, feature-gated, and backward-compatible.
- Caching: two-level caching - (1) per-instance fast LRU for compiled partial-evaluations (short TTL, e.g., 30s) and (2) shared decision cache (redis-backed) for cross-instance reuse when latency budget allows. Trade-off: consistency vs. performance; we accept eventual consistency for cache entries and include cache-miss telemetry.
- Audit-first: every decision emits an audit envelope with decision, input attributes, and evaluation path id. Envelopes are buffered and forwarded to the audit pipeline with retry/backpressure to avoid request impact.
- Explainability: store a compact "evidence vector" for denies that the console can enrich into a human-readable explanation. Keep PII out of evidence by redaction rules.

Scope and non-goals:
- Scope: API gateway enforcement, runtime middleware integration (inference runtime & control plane), console request checks, SSO/SAML attribute mapping, rollback/admin controls, audit envelope generation.
- Non-goal: full replacement of OPA-style external decision services for dedicated on-prem customers (we will provide an adapter path instead).

Acceptance criteria:
1. Decision compiler produces a binary-compatible artifact and a human-readable plan; unit tests cover compilation correctness for 200+ synthetic rule sets.
2. Sidecarless adapter added to API gateway with end-to-end perf within 1.5x baseline median latency for auth checks (target: <2ms added P50 on hosted routes).
3. Audit envelopes emitted for 100% of authorization decisions and ingested by audit pipeline with <5s tail latency in normal operation.
4. SSO/SAML mapping supports attribute-to-claims configuration and is exercised by integration tests using sample IdP assertions.
5. Emergency breakglass implemented with TTL, audit trail, and RBAC-scoped admin lock.
6. Console shows explainable deny text for common RBAC denial reasons in prod-like staging.

Implementation plan (high level):
- Phase 0 (spec): finalize rule language additions, attribute model, and audit envelope schema (Confluence: https://confluence.redwood.ai/rbac-v2/custodian-spec).
- Phase 1 (compiler): build prototype graph compiler and test harness; add fuzz tests; land in runtime-commons.
- Phase 2 (adapter): implement sidecarless adapter in API gateway and runtime middleware with feature flag.
- Phase 3 (SSO): integrate SAML attribute mapping, add integration tests with our staging IdP.
- Phase 4 (observability + admin): audit pipeline hooks, explainability service, admin override UI + canary rollout in console.
- Phase 5 (hardening): perf tuning, security review, compliance checks, and GA rollout.

Rolling and rollout strategy:
- Canary rollout to internal staging orgs first, then opt-in for early adopter customers on Hosted, then Dedicated customers via opt-in, and finally enable by default for new tenants.
- Provide a migration tool that compiles legacy RBAC v1 allow/deny lists to v2 best-effort skeletons with warnings.

Security considerations:
- Avoid storing raw SAML assertions; store only mapped attributes.
- All audit envelopes must be signed and have a tamper-evident ID.
- Admin breakglass requires two-person approval for global scopes and full audit trail retention.

Outcomes and metrics:
- Authorization P50 latency delta (target <2ms), P99 delta (target <20ms).
- Cache hit rate >70% for common workload patterns.
- Audit pipeline ingestion success >99.9% and <5s tail latency.
- Migration success rate for customer rule sets >85% with human review.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Compiler correctness via unit + fuzz tests; 2) Sidecarless adapter latency within targets; 3) 100% audit envelope emission + ingestion; 4) SAML attribute handling validated by integration tests; 5) Admin breakglass with TTL and audit; 6) Explainable denies in console UX

notes: Keep RBAC language backward-compatible where possible; provide clear migration warnings.
Consider a small interpretive VM for tenant-specific micro-expressions if compilation becomes brittle.
Plan for observability tags on decision cache hits/misses and evidence vector sizes.
